questions.stem: In the scientific method, which step comes straight after defining the problem?
options: collecting the data
choosing a research design
reviewing the literature
analysing the results
questions.explanation: The steps run: define the problem, review the literature, propose a hypothesis, choose a research design, collect data, analyse the results and draw conclusions. Reading earlier research comes before the hypothesis because the hypothesis should build on what is already known.

questions.stem: A student reads published studies on music and concentration before deciding exactly what she will predict. Why is this literature review useful?
options: It proves her prediction is right before she collects any data
It replaces the need to collect data from her own participants
It guarantees that her sample will represent the population
It shows what is known, so her hypothesis builds on it
questions.explanation: A literature review tells a researcher what earlier studies found and how they were run, so the hypothesis and design can build on them. It cannot prove a prediction or replace the researcher's own data.

questions.stem: After analysing her results, a researcher finds they do not support her hypothesis. What is the correct scientific response?
options: Repeat the study until the hypothesis is finally supported
Report that it was not supported and suggest reasons
Change the hypothesis so that it matches the results she found
Remove the participants whose scores did not fit the prediction
questions.explanation: Results that do not support a hypothesis are still findings and must be reported honestly, with possible explanations and ideas for further research. Rewriting the hypothesis afterwards or removing inconvenient data would be dishonest.

questions.stem: A research hypothesis is best described as:
options: a testable prediction about the relationship between variables
a general question about behaviour that the study will explore
a summary of the results written once the data are analysed
a statement of the procedure the participants will follow
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction about how the independent variable will affect the dependent variable in the population being studied. It is written before data are collected.

questions.stem: Which is the best-written hypothesis for an experiment on caffeine and reaction time?
options: Students who drink a cup of coffee will feel more awake and alert than they did before
Reaction time on a light-press task depends on many factors, including sleep and caffeine
Year 12 students who drink 200 mg of caffeine will react faster on a light-press task than students who drink none
Caffeine might change how people react, and this study will find out whether it does so
questions.explanation: A good hypothesis names the population, the independent variable (caffeine or none), the dependent variable (reaction time on a stated task) and the direction of the predicted effect. The others are vague, untestable or do not make a directional prediction.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the independent variable is the variable that:
options: the researcher measures to see if it changes
is kept the same for all of the participants
affects the results without being controlled
the researcher manipulates to see its effect
questions.explanation: The independent variable is deliberately changed or manipulated by the researcher. The dependent variable is what is measured, and controlled variables are kept the same.

questions.stem: Students learn a list of 20 words either in silence or with music playing, and the number of words recalled is counted. What is the dependent variable?
options: the number of words recalled
whether music is played
the list of 20 chosen words
the time given to learn them
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the measured outcome, here the number of words recalled. Whether music is played is the independent variable, and the word list and learning time should be controlled.

questions.stem: In an experiment on whether exercise improves mood, one group walks for 30 minutes and another group sits reading for 30 minutes. The group that reads is the:
options: stratified group
control group
experimental group
placebo group
questions.explanation: The control group is not exposed to the independent variable (exercise), giving a baseline for comparison. The walking group is the experimental group.

questions.stem: In a study of a new study app, one class uses the app and another class, taught by a different teacher, does not. The app class scores higher. Why can the researcher not conclude the app caused the difference?
options: The teacher is an uncontrolled variable that differs by group
The app class is the control group, so its scores cannot be compared
The dependent variable was not measured in the class that used the app
Two classes is too many groups for a valid experimental comparison
questions.explanation: Because the two groups had different teachers, the teacher varies along with the independent variable and could explain the difference. An uncontrolled variable that varies systematically with the independent variable is a confounding variable.

questions.stem: A placebo is:
options: a fake treatment that has no active effect
a treatment given only to the experimental group
a variable that changes along with the IV
a measure of how strongly two variables relate
questions.explanation: A placebo looks like the real treatment but has no active ingredient or effect, such as a sugar pill. It is given to the control group so that both groups believe they may be receiving treatment.

questions.stem: Participants in a control group are given a sugar pill that they believe is a memory-boosting drug, and their recall improves. This improvement is best explained as:
options: a placebo effect caused by their expectations
an experimenter effect caused by the researcher
a sampling error caused by an unequal sample
an order effect caused by repeated testing
questions.explanation: The placebo effect is a change in the participant's behaviour caused by their belief or expectation about a treatment, not the treatment itself. The sugar pill has no active effect, so the improvement comes from expectation.

questions.stem: In a single-blind study:
options: participants do not know which condition they are in
the researcher does not know which condition is which
neither participants nor researcher know the conditions
participants are not told the study is taking place
questions.explanation: In a single-blind procedure only the participants are unaware of whether they are in the experimental or control condition. This controls the placebo effect but not the experimenter effect.

questions.stem: A researcher who expects a drug to work rates the anxiety of participants in a trial. Why would a double-blind procedure improve this study?
options: The researcher could then measure two dependent variables at once
The researcher's expectations could not bias the ratings of each group
The participants would not need to give informed consent before starting
The sample would become more representative of the target population
questions.explanation: In a double-blind procedure neither the participants nor the person collecting data knows who received the real drug. This controls the experimenter effect as well as the placebo effect, because the researcher cannot treat or rate the groups differently.

questions.stem: A random sample is one in which:
options: the researcher chooses the people most likely to support the hypothesis
every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected
participants are chosen because they are easy for the researcher to reach
the population is divided into groups and each group is sampled in turn
questions.explanation: In random sampling every member of the population has an equal chance of selection, for example by drawing names from a full list. This makes it less likely that the sample is biased.

questions.stem: A student surveys the first 30 people she meets in the school library at lunchtime. This is:
options: a stratified sample
a random sample
a matched-pairs sample
an opportunistic sample
questions.explanation: An opportunistic (convenience) sample uses whoever is available at the time. It is quick and easy but rarely represents the whole population, because people in the library may differ from other students.

questions.stem: A school has 60% girls and 40% boys. A researcher wants a sample of 50 that matches this. How many boys should be in a stratified sample?
questions.explanation: In a stratified sample each subgroup appears in the same proportion as in the population. Forty per cent of 50 is 20 boys, so the sample has 30 girls and 20 boys.

questions.stem: Why is stratified sampling often preferred to opportunistic sampling for a survey of attitudes in a school?
options: It means that every student in the school will be included in the survey
It ensures key subgroups appear in the same proportions as the population
It allows the researcher to choose the most willing and helpful participants
It removes the need to ask the participants for their informed consent
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling deliberately represents important subgroups, such as year levels, in their population proportions, so results can be generalised more confidently. An opportunistic sample may over-represent whoever happens to be available.

questions.stem: An in-depth study of one person, often over a long period and using several sources of information, is called:
options: a secondary source
a case study
a survey
an experiment
questions.explanation: A case study investigates one individual or a small group in great depth, using interviews, observation, records and tests. It gives rich detail but its findings may not generalise to others.

questions.stem: A researcher watches and records how often children share toys in a kindergarten, without interfering. This is:
options: a structured interview of the children
a survey using a rating scale
a naturalistic observational study
a controlled laboratory experiment
questions.explanation: In a naturalistic observation behaviour is watched and recorded in its usual setting without the researcher intervening. This gives realistic behaviour but cannot show cause and effect.

questions.stem: Which is the main advantage of the experimental method over other methods of data collection?
options: It can study one rare individual in very great depth
It can show cause and effect between variables
It always takes place in the participants' natural settings
It produces rich descriptions of each person's experiences
questions.explanation: Because the researcher manipulates the independent variable and controls other variables, an experiment can show that one variable causes a change in another. Observations, surveys and case studies can describe behaviour but not show cause.

questions.stem: A student uses Australian Bureau of Statistics data on hours of sleep reported by teenagers. This is an example of:
options: a primary source of data
a case study of teenagers
a single-blind sleep survey
a secondary source of data
questions.explanation: Secondary data were collected by someone else for another purpose and are reused by the researcher. Primary data are collected first-hand by the researcher for the current study.

questions.stem: Which pair gives one qualitative and one quantitative measure, in that order?
options: a score out of 10 on a rating scale; the number of words a participant recalled
an interview transcript of a student; a diary entry about that person's daily mood
a participant's description of feeling nervous; their heart rate in beats per minute
the number of errors made; the time taken in seconds
questions.explanation: Qualitative data are descriptions of qualities, such as feelings expressed in words. Quantitative data are numbers, such as heart rate. Error counts, times and rating scores are all quantitative, and transcripts and diaries are both qualitative.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to know how Year 12 students feel about exam pressure, in their own words. Which method best suits this aim?
options: a controlled experiment with a placebo condition
a survey of yes or no questions sent to every school
a count of absences in the week before the exams
semi-structured interviews with open-ended questions
questions.explanation: Open-ended interview questions let participants describe their experiences in their own words, producing rich qualitative data. Yes or no questions and absence counts give quantitative data that cannot capture how students feel.

questions.stem: In a study, 18 of 24 participants recalled the target word. What percentage is this?
Five participants recalled 6, 9, 7, 10 and 8 words. What is the mean number of words recalled?
questions.explanation: The mean is the sum divided by the number of scores: (6 + 9 + 7 + 10 + 8) / 5 = 40 / 5 = 8.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to show how mean reaction time changed over six hours without sleep, measured every hour. Which graph suits this best?
options: a line graph
a pie chart
a bar chart of categories
a frequency table
questions.explanation: A line graph shows how a continuous measure changes over time or across ordered intervals. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and bar charts compare separate categories.

questions.stem: A survey asks students which of four ways they mainly travel to school. Which display best shows the share of students using each way?
options: a pie chart
a line graph
a scatter of points
a correlation coefficient
questions.explanation: A pie chart shows how a whole (all the students surveyed) divides into categories, so each slice is a percentage of the total. A line graph suits change across time.

questions.stem: A correlation coefficient of +0.85 between hours of study and exam score shows:
options: a strong negative relationship
a weak positive relationship
no relationship at all
a strong positive relationship
questions.explanation: The sign shows direction and the size shows strength. A value close to +1 means a strong positive relationship: more study goes with higher scores.

questions.stem: Four studies of sleep and mood report the correlations below. Which study found the strongest relationship?
questions.explanation: Strength depends on how close the value is to 1 or −1, regardless of sign. −0.78 is furthest from zero, so it is the strongest, even though the relationship is negative.

questions.stem: A study finds a correlation of +0.70 between hours of screen time and reported anxiety in teenagers. Which conclusion is valid?
options: Reducing screen time will lower anxiety in every teenager
Teenagers with more screen time tend to report more anxiety
Screen time causes teenagers to become more anxious over time
Anxiety causes teenagers to spend more time looking at screens
questions.explanation: A correlation shows the variables are related, not which causes which. A third variable could cause both, so only the statement describing the relationship is valid.

questions.stem: A study has high external validity when:
options: its results can be generalised to other people and settings
it measured what it claimed to be measuring
its results are the same each time the test is given
participants were unaware of their assigned condition
questions.explanation: External validity is about generalisation: whether the findings apply beyond the particular sample and setting to the wider population and real life. Measuring what was intended relates to internal validity.

questions.stem: A study of memory used 20 volunteer university students in a laboratory. A critic says the results may not apply to older adults. The critic is questioning the study's:
options: control group
dependent variable
external validity
use of a placebo
questions.explanation: Whether results apply to people outside the sample, such as older adults, is a question of external validity. A small, unrepresentative volunteer sample limits generalisation.

questions.stem: Informed consent means that participants:
options: have their names kept separate from their results
agree to take part after being told what it involves
are told the true aim of the study only after it has ended
can leave the study at any time without giving a reason
questions.explanation: Informed consent is agreement to participate given after the nature, purpose and risks of the study have been explained. For people under 18, a parent or guardian usually also gives consent.

questions.stem: Halfway through a study, a participant says she no longer wants to continue. The researcher should:
options: let her leave and remove her data if she asks
ask her to finish so that the data are complete
allow her to leave but still use all her results
offer her a reward if she agrees to stay on
questions.explanation: Withdrawal rights allow participants to leave at any time without penalty, and to have their results removed. Pressuring her to stay or using her data against her wishes would breach ethical principles.

questions.stem: A participant's survey answers are stored under a code number, and the list linking names to codes is locked away. This protects:
options: debriefing
voluntary participation
external validity
confidentiality
questions.explanation: Confidentiality means participants' personal information and results are protected and not identifiable to others. Coding data and securing the link between names and codes protects it.

questions.stem: A researcher tells participants the study is about eyesight when it is really about conformity. Under what condition is this deception acceptable?
options: The participants are adults and were paid for the time they spent in the study
The researcher records the deception later in the results section of the report
The participants have already signed a form agreeing to take part in the study
It is needed for valid results, causes no harm and is followed by a debriefing
questions.explanation: Deception is used only when knowing the true aim would change participants' behaviour, when it carries no risk of harm, and when it is approved and followed by a full debriefing. Payment or signing a consent form does not justify it.

questions.stem: Debriefing at the end of a study involves:
options: asking participants to sign the consent form for the study
assigning participants to the control or experimental group
storing participants' results under a code number
explaining the true aims and correcting any false beliefs
questions.explanation: Debriefing occurs after participation: the researcher explains the real purpose, reveals any deception, answers questions and ensures participants leave in no worse state than they arrived.

questions.stem: What is the main role of a human research ethics committee?
options: to select a random sample of participants from the target population
to publish the results once the study has been completed and checked
to review a planned study and approve it only if it is ethical
to collect the data so that the researcher cannot bias the results
questions.explanation: An ethics committee reviews research proposals before they begin, weighing risks against benefits and checking for consent, confidentiality, withdrawal rights and debriefing. Research cannot start without its approval.

questions.stem: Researchers propose a study on the effects of stress hormones in rats. Which requirement reflects ethical guidelines for animal research?
options: The animals must be released into the wild once the study has finished
The benefits must justify any harm, and suffering must be kept to a minimum
Animals may be used freely because ethical guidelines apply only to humans
Animals must give consent through trained responses before they take part
questions.explanation: Animal research must be approved by an animal ethics committee, be justified by its likely benefits, use as few animals as possible and minimise pain and distress. Ethical guidelines do apply to animals.

questions.stem: Which is part of the experimenter's ethical responsibility for participants' wellbeing?
options: choosing participants who will support the hypothesis
stopping the study if a participant shows distress
making sure every participant completes all of the tasks
keeping the true results secret from the ethics committee
questions.explanation: The experimenter is responsible for participants' welfare throughout the study and must stop or modify procedures if harm or distress appears. Participants can withdraw at any time.
